doc.title: Larry Ridley interviewed by Monk Rowe, Toronto, Canada, January 10, 2003

title: Thanks, and retirement from Rutgers after 28 years
summary: Mutual thanks, then Ridley describes building Rutgers's jazz degree programs and hiring tenured Black faculty.

story.theme_name: Teaching jazz: schools, students and advice to the young
story.community_name: Becoming a teacher: jazz in schools and conservatories

blocks.x: Man, you have given me some great food for thought today.

Well I thank you for asking me to come, and I hope this is not the last time we have an opportunity — I hope we are able to interact on many different — you know doing workshops and clinics and whatever.
Whatever way, just call me and just say, “Hey, what’s happening?”
I know you retired very recently from —

1999, I was retired after 28 years at Rutgers. I build the undergraduate degree program there, and the master’s program there in jazz. I helped shepherd that. And I was very fortunate in that I was the first and only, at that time, and I don’t know if it’s changing now but I had four tenured professors in jazz. And four of them African-American. The first person I brought in was Ted Dunbar. Second person Kenny Baron. Then Bill Fielder and then of course myself. And had a lot of great people who came through there teaching and sharing there, from Don Friedman and Frank Foster to, oh God if I start naming names I’m liable to leave somebody out. But Milt Jackson, and great artists in residence. I started a lot of that stuff doing the music of — and I would have thematic presentation where the ensemble would perform the music of Charlie Parker, the music of this, and I’m continuing forth with that too.
